notes: ordinary meaning of English words: commonly used meanings unless the context demands otherwise
preamble: provisions amplify the philosophy summarised in the Preamble; of multiple interpretations the one that best fits the Preamble's philosophy is correct

progressive interpretation: norms change, so read provisions with changing social norms and emerging conditions; e.g. Article 21 from restrictive to expansive meaning of life, giving shelter to many rights
purposive interpretation: uses the purpose or intent (Constituent Assembly Debates); read in light of the entire Constitution, an ecosystem in itself, and all parts read together
harmonious construction: where one provision conflicts with another, reconcile them and give maximum possible effect
liberal interpretation: provisions on liberty and security of citizens interpreted in their favour; e.g. privacy, freedom of the press, RTI through Articles 19 and 21

body: Threats: Obsolete laws · Politicians · Judiciary · Media and publishers · Officials. (own mnemonic)

Heckler's Veto: the threat of disruption or violence by one group effectively silences a speaker. The remedy (Rangarajan): the State must protect lawful expression and keep order, not give in to the heckler.

meta.title: Freedom OF Speech AND Expression · Significance · Balance · Threats
meta.toc: Significance of freedom of speech; balancing; threats
meta.pyq: None quoted in the handout · Fundamental Rights handout pp. 27-28
meta.simple: Speech has value in itself, keeps democracy accountable, builds community, drives change and the marketplace of ideas. Restrictions must be proportionate; err on the side of freedom. Threats: old laws, weak politicians, weak courts, compliant media, Heckler's Veto, pliant officials.
recall: free contest of ideas refines them
two-wheeler ban for accidents is over-restriction

notes: press freedom is not named in the Constitution; it is inferred from Art 19(1)(a)
NCRWC recommended explicit recognition in Art 19

notes.h: Role of media in a democracy

notes: civic forum: a "parliament of citizens"; public discussion, debate, criticism
watchdog: speaks truth to power; more press freedom, more accountability; modern democracy is mediated
adversarial relationship (slightly) with government is a sign of health
protective: voice to the voiceless, helps welfare of weaker sections
information: censorship leaves citizens, then government, less informed and weakens feedback
value creation: brings attention to disasters and neglected issues (health facilities, malnutrition, road accidents, schools) and shapes what the government treats as important

body: Roles: Civic forum · Watchdog · Adversarial · Protective · Information · Value-setting. (own mnemonic)

Amartya Sen's example: in the Great Chinese Famine (1958-61), censorship meant even officials lacked reliable information on the crisis; absence of free information and criticism worsened the disaster. A free press helps governments see and answer suffering.

notes: many registered publications and channels suggest a vibrant space, but numbers do not prove freedom

World Press Freedom Index (RSF) ranks countries; India's ranking raises questions on journalist safety, political pressure, institutional conditions. Rank figures in the lecture are year-specific, not the present rank (check current RSF)
readership and viewership concentrated in a few entities; easier for the powerful to influence
owners have other businesses and dealings with government (contracts, approvals) and links with parties
Murdochisation: one entity dominating print, TV and radio; reduces diversity; limits on cross-media concentration argued for

Paid news: payment-influenced content presented as news; candidates and outlets collude; small papers vulnerable; raises election-expenditure questions; not a separate offence under the RPA 1951 by that label, though conduct may fall under other laws
Conflict of interest: outlets holding equity in businesses they then cover
media acts as judge, jury and executioner: a Kangaroo Court (body without legitimate authority acting as a court); Khap Panchayats criticised similarly
reputation (Art 21 dignity): guilty before the verdict
privacy: excessive reporting of personal details
fair trial: pressure on the judiciary, loss of presumption of innocence, interference with administration of justice

body: Sahara India Real Estate v. SEBI (2012): Doctrine of Postponement. If immediate reporting creates a real and substantial risk to a fair trial, the court may order a temporary postponement, with strict safeguards: necessary and proportionate. Criticism: may deny the right to know, does not curb frivolous media behaviour, can shield influential accused; balance fair trial with public information.

notes: "Good news is no news": chase for ads and TRPs fuels sensationalism
the Chinese Wall between editorial and marketing has been breached (it should stop commercial pressure on editorial decisions)
exclusive stories chased for TRPs
breaking news on unfinished stories: inaccuracy
commodification: serious news packaged as entertainment
yellow journalism: little researched content, sensational headlines
gonzo journalism: reporter becomes part of the story; deliberately subjective, not necessarily unethical
post-truth: emotion and belief outweigh objective facts

need better education and training standards without hurting independence

notes: derived mainly from Art 19(1)(a) (speech) and 19(1)(b) (assembly); connected to 19(1)(c) (association)
protests concern life, livelihood, dignity, so also linked to Art 21
since parent rights are subject to reasonable restrictions, so is protest; the task is balancing peaceful protest with public order and others' rights

body: Protest roots: Art 19(1)(a) speech · 19(1)(b) assembly · 19(1)(c) association, plus Art 21. (own mnemonic)

head: Case
Held
rows: Himat Lal K. Shah v. Commissioner of Police (1973)
assembly right is not an unrestricted right to protest anywhere, any way; State may regulate meetings and processions, but no general or arbitrary ban on peaceful assemblies in all public places
expression cannot be suppressed on illusory, imaginary or remote threats to public order; need a proximate connection with anticipated harm
Amit Sahni v. Commissioner of Police (2020) (Shaheen Bagh)
protest must be balanced with public order and others' rights; no indefinite occupation or blockage of public roads; State may regulate place and manner

notes: disruption is natural to many protests; society must show reasonable tolerance of inconvenience, else the right becomes hollow
but public inconvenience is not an extra ground in Art 19(3); any restriction must be justified within the Constitution and law

body: Balance: assembly is a Fundamental Right; restrict only within constitutional limits; protect democratic mobilisation and dissent as well as public order.

July 2026 magazine, "Right to Protest": the NEET protest march; the SC observed that peaceful protest is guaranteed. Cases listed there: Ramlila Maidan (2012), MKSS (2018) (designated protest sites in Delhi), Anuradha Bhasin (internet access), Shaheen Bagh (2020). Prelims fodder: Art 19 is for citizens only; "public order" was inserted by the First Amendment, 1951.

September 2026 magazine: the SC used Art 142 to quash FIRs against students in the NEET-UG 2026 protest. PYQ 2019 on Art 142 and PYQs on free speech, hate speech and films are noted there. Check the order before quoting.

meta.simple: Protest is derived from Arts 19(1)(a), (b), (c) and linked to Art 21. It is subject to reasonable restrictions. Amit Sahni (Shaheen Bagh) says no indefinite blocking of roads; Himat Lal says no unrestricted right but no blanket ban; Rangarajan needs a proximate link to harm.

proximate link needed; no illusory threats
Shaheen Bagh; no indefinite road blockage
